extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, proofreaders, and publishers preparing/managing scholarly and technical manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for spelling, abbreviations, and punctuation (periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, quotation marks, apostrophes, etc.) for preparing clear, consistent scholarly/technical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for weights, measures, and metric symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The common designations of weights and measures in the metric system, as well as the symbols of measurement in common use, when following a numeral (e.g., 1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; gm. = gram; lb. = pound; kg. = kilogram; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed standard abbreviations when they follow numerals; examples provided include sq. mi., gm., gr., h., min., sec., oz., yd., ft., in., kw., mg., A (angstrom units), C. (Centrigrade), F. (Fahrenheit). See also note (See 123.) regarding periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended technical-value abbreviations (AIEE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the standard abbreviations for technical values recommended by the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (e.g., a-c., b.h.p., boiler h.p., B.t.u., c-p., cm., cu., d-c., e.h.p., e.m.f., ft., gal., g., gm., hr., in., i.h.p., kg., km., kw., kw-hr., m.m.f., mm., min., m., m-kg., rev. per min., r.p.m., sec., sq., kv., kv-a., watt-hr., watts per c-p., yd.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these industry-standard abbreviations in technical contexts. Note: in hyphenated abbreviations the first element of the compound does not take a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenated abbreviation punctuation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of hyphenated abbreviations, the first element of the compound does not take a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., use 'kw-hr.' not 'kw.-hr.'; follow this rule consistently for hyphenated abbreviated compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use office style vs. literal original in extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ but slightly from ours, and where such variations do not affect the meaning, use office style; in citations from Old English works or when a faithful rendering is essential, follow the original copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should always be accurately quoted. (Rule 112.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming possessives of proper names ending in sibilants
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if monosyllabic, add an apostrophe and s; if of more than one syllable, add an apostrophe only (except names ending in -ce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions.' See exceptions for silent sibilants (Charlevoix's, Des Moines's). (Rule 113.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive for names ending in silent sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: For proper names ending in a silent sibilant, form the possessive by adding the apostrophe and s, whether the word is monosyllabic or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population.' (Continuation of Rule 113.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite article 'a' before sounded h, long u, 'one', 'once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h, long u (or eu), and the words 'one,' 'once,' use 'a' as the indefinite article (e.g., a hotel, a historical work, a euphonious word, such a one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 114.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligatures usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The ligatures æ and œ are not used at the present day in Latin/Greek words or words adopted into English; write ae, oe, or e alone. The ligature is retained, however, in Old English and in French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'aetas; Oedipus Tyrannus; aesthetic; (but: oeuvre, French); but: maneuver; Alfred (Alfred in English).' (Rule 115.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Farther vs. further distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further' by using the former in the sense of 'more remote,' 'at a greater distance'; the latter in the sense of 'moreover,' 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.' (Rule 116.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocative 'O' and exclamatory 'Oh' punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use the 'O' without a comma following; for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma or an exclamation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did he not...?' (Rule 117.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles retaining or omitting final '-e'
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final e in the primary word (agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing, eyeing, shoeing, vieing); others omit the e before the terminal (abridging, acknowledging, aging, arguing, awing, biting, bluing, changing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lists as guidance when forming participles from base verbs. (Rule 118.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spellings list
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the provided standard spellings for many common variant words (e.g., abridgment, acknowledgment, adz, aegis, Aeolian, aesthetic, afterward, almanac, ambassador, among, anemia, appareled, appendixes (of book), arbor, archaeology, ardor, armor, ... up through 'saber').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the manual's preferred variant spellings consistently in copy. The list is extensive—consult it for each specific word. (Rule 119.)

rubrics_metrics.name: One-word forms and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make one word of 'anyone,' 'everyone,' 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'cannot'. Distinguish between 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)', 'someone' vs 'some one (or more) of the number.' Use the form 'someone else's.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In medical work, 'technic' may be more generally spelled 'technic' (note). (Following Rule 119.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of -ise vs -ize terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the terminations -ise and -ize according to the manual's lists: certain verbs/spellings are given under 'SPELL WITH -ise' (e.g., advertise, advise, apprise, comprise, etc.), and many under 'SPELL WITH -ize' (e.g., aggrandize, agonize, analyze, emphasize, dramatize, energize, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided lists to determine whether to spell with -ise or -ize; the manual enumerates many examples. (Rule 120.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation font/style matching
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show punctuation matching preceding type style: 'With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill'; Luke 4:16a; paragraph 2 (a). (Rule 121.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Period indicates end of declarative sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a declarative sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 122.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations, not after contractions; metric/chemical exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: a) Put a period after all abbreviations (Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. i, Chas., ibid., S.V., 10 mm.). b) Do not use a period after contractions (use apostrophe to indicate omitted letters). c) Treat metric symbols as abbreviations and use periods; do not use periods after chemical symbols, 'per cent', nor book format abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exceptions given: O, Fe; 2 per cent; 4to, 8vo. Note exceptions for technical matters and recognized abbreviations for linguistic epochs, publication initials, and MS (no period). (Rule 123.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals (Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 124.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running heads and many headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence, date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 125.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of period relative to quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is always placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter enclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a rule without exception. Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' Put the period inside the quotation marks. When parentheses form part of the preceding sentence, put the period outside. (Rule 126.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point marks an outcry, an emphatic or ironical utterance. It is placed inside quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quotation or parenthetical matter; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' and illustrated placements when quoting. (Rules 127-128.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point (question mark) usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query or to express a doubt. Indirect questions should not be followed by a question mark. Technically interrogative sentences disguised as courtesy requests do not need the interrogation point. Place the question mark inside quotation marks or parentheses only when it is part of the quoted/parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' ; indirect: He asked whether he was ill. 'Will you kindly sign and return the inclosed card.' (Rules 129-130.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon—functions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period and is commonly used (i) to emphasize close connection between two clauses each a complete sentence, (ii) to separate a complete clause from a second that illustrates or amplifies it, and (iii) to introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before quotation of a clause in the middle of a sentence use a comma. Numerous examples provided. (Rule 131.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon vs comma after introductory words like 'namely' or 'for instance'
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon often takes the place of an implied 'namely,' 'as follows,' 'for instance.' Use a colon if what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses; otherwise use a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast: 'This is true of only two nations — the wealthiest...: Great Britain and France' (colon) vs 'This is true of only two nations — viz., Great Britain and France' (comma after 'viz.'). (Rule 132.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutations and addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter, and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or the audience ('My dear Mr. Brown:'; 'Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 133.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Centered colon use in scripture/time/refs
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a centered colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, between hours and minutes in time indications, and between volume and page reference when such style is used (e.g., Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.; Botanical Gazette 20:144).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 134.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between place and publisher in bibliographic refs
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary and bibliographical references (e.g., Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 135.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless it is a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: He writes under the head of 'Notes and Comments': 'Many a man can testify...'. (Rule 136.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon—use for stronger division than comma
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma; it often separates clauses closely related but standing as separate units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show use in complex sentences and guidance that 'for' in such cases should commonly be preceded by a semicolon. (Rule 137.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between the different links if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, especially if individual clauses contain punctuation of lesser value than a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long enumerations with internal punctuation should use semicolons to separate items. Examples given including membership lists and multi-clause defenses. (Rule 138.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters (e.g., Gen. 2:3-6, 9, 14; 3:17; chap. 5; 6:15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 139.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon placement relative to quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon should be placed outside the quotation marks or parentheses, unless it is part of the quotation or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 140.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma—general function
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive examples demonstrate how commas affect meaning and rhythm; the comma is a primary device for clarity. (Rule 141.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separating proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places ('To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 142.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (Oxford) comma guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and', 'or', and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or all the links in a longer series; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not use a comma where 'and' serves to connect all links in a brief and close-knit phrase. Examples illustrate both cases. (Rule 143.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions such as 'and', 'but', 'if', 'while', 'as', 'whereas', 'since', 'because', 'when', 'after', 'although', especially if a change of subject takes place; but do not when the preceding clause is not logically complete without them or when phrases are brief and close-welded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show where commas are required and where omitted for close-knit phrases. (Rule 144.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with introductory adverbial/connective words
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions/adverbs/phrases like 'now', 'then', 'however', 'indeed', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'nevertheless', 'though', 'in short', 'for instance', etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause and set off by commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence to mark a distinct break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a comma with such words when the connection is logically close and structurally smooth (examples given). (Rule 145.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma before 'rather' in certain expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 146.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between adjectives when last adjective relates more directly
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the admirable political institutions of the country'; 'a handsome, wealthy young man.' (Rule 147.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma setting off participial clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those containing an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone.' (Rule 148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause or phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them, but because...' (Rule 149.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional interpolations; use dashes for stronger breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use the two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast comma-set interpolations with dash-set strong interruptions. (Rule 150.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between identical or similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words even if grammatical construction does not require separation (e.g., 'Whatever is, is good').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 151.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with complementary/delimiting adjectival phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should ordinarily be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though at the same time perfectly logical, conclusion.' (Rule 152.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separating coordinate clauses modifying a later clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more coordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate coordination and comma separation. (Rule 153.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate numbers or thousands separators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers in text and to mark thousands (e.g., 1,276; 10,419), except in dates or page-references; do not separate constituents of dimensions, weights, measures (e.g., 3 feet 6 inches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions for certain journals that do not use a comma with four figures. (Rules 154, 159.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with omitted words (ellipsis by omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two.' But often such constructions are smooth enough not to call for commas. (Rule 155.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before brief direct quotations/maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.' (Rule 156.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' with residence/position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position (e.g., Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.; President Hadley, of Yale University). Exceptions where place-name is effectively part of name (Clement of Alexandria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 157.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma vs en dash in consecutive vs continuous references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references insert a comma between consecutive numbers to represent a break in continuity (pp. 4, 7-8, 10); use an en dash to represent a continuous reference between consecutive numbers (IV, 123-30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 158.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement in date expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year, and similar time divisions, by a comma (e.g., November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions in some journals (Astrophysical Journal, Botanical Gazette). (Rule 160.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures and lead lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after an author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after an address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 161.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following the parenthesis if the context requires it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 162.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for contractions and omitted figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number. In contractions containing a verb and the negative, do not use a space between the two components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: it's, ne'er, 'twas, 't isn't; m'f'g; the class of '96; don't, haven't. (Rule 163.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming possessive case with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s according to the possessive rules (see 113).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms. (Rule 164.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals and of rare or artificial noun-coinages is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, by adding an apostrophe alone (monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others, s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in two's and three's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; the Pericles' and Socrates' of literature. (Rule 165.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash—use to denote abrupt break or emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash denotes a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, an abrupt change in construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected/epigrammatic turn of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do we — can we — send out educated boys...' ; 'To be or not to be — that is the question.' (Rule 166.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dashes for independent parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This may be said to be — but, never mind, we will pass over that.' (Rule 167.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce emphatic explanatory clause repeating phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas.' (Rule 168.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dash when 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons...' (Rule 169.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final—summarizing—clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates summary clause preceded by dash. (Rule 170.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after a heading word followed by paragraph list
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash (e.g., 'I recommend — 1. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 171.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash in side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 172.)
